prize_parts.citation: for the development of targeted protein degradation, in which small molecules recruit E3 ubiquitin ligases to destroy chosen proteins, through PROTACs and the molecular-glue mechanism of thalidomide analogues

statement.case_for: Targeted protein degradation is the most broadly supported candidate on the table (two first places, six top-three rankings, ranked by all eight members), and I now put it first. It introduced a genuinely new pharmacological principle: event-driven, catalytic removal of a protein rather than occupancy-based inhibition, which reaches targets that were considered undruggable. The chemistry is concrete: heterobifunctional design, ternary-complex cooperativity, and the cereblon mechanism that explained how thalidomide analogues act as molecular glues. Crews and Deshaies conceived and demonstrated the PROTAC concept, and Handa and Ito identified cereblon as the thalidomide target, which is the mechanistic root of the glue strand. The mechanism has been confirmed independently in many laboratories and many degraders are in clinical trials. My own field is nucleotide metabolism and DNA replication, so I place sequencing, which I ranked first, as a close and fully mature alternative rather than as the lead.
statement.case_against: No PROTAC has yet been approved, so the clinical payoff that would make recognition uncontroversial is still pending, and the work may be somewhat early. The attribution is also hard to fit in three names. Ciulli (structure-guided VHL-based design), Ito, Gray, Sakamoto and Kim all contributed important pieces, and choosing between the cereblon-glue strand and the VHL/structure strand is partly a judgement about what the prize is for. Sequencing is the opposite case: mature and overdue, but its credit is spread across Solexa, 454 and other platforms, and the 2002 and 2020 prizes recognized adjacent areas.

responses.point: Aili ranks B020 first as an original, translationally consequential modality with Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli, and notes that the cereblon/molecular-glue strand fits awkwardly into three names.
responses.response: I agree on the scientific merit and on the awkwardness of the three-name limit, but I would give the third place to Handa rather than Ciulli. The cereblon discovery is what explained thalidomide and gave the glue mechanism, and it is the strand that cannot be recovered from the PROTAC concept paper alone. Ciulli's structure-guided VHL work is a strong refinement of a design principle that Crews and Deshaies had already shown. I accept that this is a judgement call, and I do not think the committee should settle it on opening support alone.

responses.point: Brzezinski puts perovskite solar absorbers first, citing rapid efficiency gains, wide replication and large energy impact, while acknowledging that stability and commercialization are unresolved.
responses.response: Perovskites are a real chemical success, and the efficiency numbers are reproducible. My reservation is the one he names himself: stability, lead content and manufacturing are open, and the prize should not be awarded on the promise of an application. Degradation has the opposite weakness, since its mechanism is well established and only the approvals are pending. I would therefore rank perovskites as a serious second-tier candidate that may mature later, rather than ahead of B020.

responses.point: Linke, the chair, puts B020 first and B014 second, calling sequencing fully mature and overdue, though he suggests only Balasubramanian and Klenerman as the core.
responses.response: We agree on the order of the top two, and I agree with a two-name core for sequencing, which is closer to the chemistry than adding Rothberg. I did place sequencing first myself, so I am not downplaying it. I put degradation first here only because it has the broader support and a cleaner attribution to named inventors, while the sequencing credit would need a decision about whether pyrosequencing and semiconductor sequencing belong in the prize. If the committee prefers a mature, overdue topic over an emerging one, B014 is where I would go.

responses.point: Sparr ranks ionizable lipid nanoparticles first for their global clinical validation, and ranks phase separation second as a physical-chemical organizing principle, noting its in vivo relevance is debated.
responses.response: I share her view that lipid nanoparticles are mature and chemically well founded, which is why I keep B049 as an alternative. My concern is the 2023 Medicine prize for nucleoside-modified mRNA, which makes a chemistry prize on the delivery vehicle look like a second recognition of the same vaccines, and the credit among Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Langer and Anderson is spread across many people. On condensates I agree with her caution: the in vitro physical chemistry is solid, but the disagreement about physiological function means I would not rank B027 above degradation at this stage.

uncertainties: Whether a prize should recognize PROTACs and molecular glues together, and if so how to divide the three names among Crews, Deshaies, Handa and Ciulli
Whether the absence of an approved degrader drug makes the timing too early
Whether sequencing credit can be limited to Balasubramanian, Klenerman and possibly Rothberg without ignoring Mayer and Ju
How much weight the 2023 Medicine mRNA prize should carry against a lipid nanoparticle prize
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My work on dNTP pools and ribonucleotide reductase is adjacent to the nucleotide chemistry in sequencing (B014), but I have no documented personal or institutional tie to any shortlisted candidate. My collaborators named in the profile are not candidates, so I do not see a need for recusal.
